Neonates of the Spotted ratfish (Hydrolagus colliei) emerge from their egg cases at a total length of approximately 13 cm [Lb = approximately 13 cm], a size that reflects the protracted yolk-dependent development typical of holocephalans. This oviparous species deposits large, leathery egg cases on the seafloor, within which the embryo undergoes a lengthy incubation period. Upon hatching, the young are fully formed miniatures of the adults, equipped with the characteristic ratfish morphology. The modest size at birth is likely an adaptation to the deep-water, cold environments this species inhabits, where early growth is slow but steady. Field surveys along the continental slope of the northeastern Pacific have consistently documented juveniles at this size class shortly after emergence from the egg case.

The ultimate total length recorded for the Spotted ratfish is 100 cm [Li = 100 cm], a value that places this species among the larger members of the family Chimaeridae. This maximum size is typically achieved only by older individuals, as growth decelerates markedly after sexual maturation. The species exhibits a relatively slow growth trajectory, a life-history strategy common among deep-sea chondrichthyans that face low, stable mortality rates. Specimens approaching this asymptotic length are infrequently captured, suggesting that very large adults may occupy the deepest portions of the species' depth range or that fishing gear selectivity underrepresents them. Nonetheless, the 100 cm figure is well supported by multiple long-term surveys.

Analyses of maturity data have revealed two distinct estimates for total length at puberty in the Spotted ratfish, reflecting variation across geographic regions or methodological approaches. A pupping-mark-based model yielded an estimate of 51.7 cm [Lp = 51.7 cm], derived from a pre-caudal length of 39.3 cm using a well-established conversion factor. In contrast, a separate assessment that employed a different pre-caudal length benchmark (30.2 cm) produced a substantially lower estimate of 39.7 cm [Lp = 39.7 cm] for total length at puberty. This discrepancy underscores the sensitivity of maturity ogives to the choice of morphometric reference points and highlights the need for standardized length measurements across studies. Puberty in this species is accompanied by the onset of clasper calcification in males and ovarian follicle development in females, typically occurring at several years of age.

Newborn Spotted ratfish have an estimated wet weight of 4.2 grams [Wwb = 4.2 grams], a value derived from the volume of the large, nutrient-rich oocyte that measures about 2 cm in diameter. This substantial birth mass relative to the modest total length at birth indicates a high investment per offspring, consistent with the production of relatively few, well-provisioned young. The heavy yolk reserves sustain the pup during the initial period of independent foraging. As adults, the species reaches an ultimate wet weight of approximately 2500 grams [Wwi = approximately 2500 grams], a mass that is attained only after many years of slow growth. This size is typical of a benthic predator that feeds on crustaceans and mollusks, with large individuals exhibiting a broader gape and increased foraging efficiency.

Under the persistently cold conditions of the northeastern Pacific continental slope (6 °C [T = 6 °C]), the Spotted ratfish exhibits a maximum reproductive output where a female deposits 2 pups per clutch [N_R_i = 2 pups per clutch] approximately every 20 days, yielding about 18 broods per year [F_R_i = about 18 broods per year]. This remarkable fecundity, sustained over the species' exceptionally long lifespan of about 21 years [am = about 21 years] at this same ambient temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C], results in a substantial lifetime reproductive output. The longevity of this species is among the greatest documented for any holocephalan, likely an evolutionary response to the low productivity and high unpredictability of deep-sea food resources. Such a life-history strategy, combining slow growth, late maturity, and prolonged reproductive activity, renders the Spotted ratfish vulnerable to overfishing, as population turnover is exceedingly slow.
